parts: Go to your fridge. Pick up a yogurt, and then a pack of chicken.
Both have a date. But read the words. One says best before. The other says use by.
They look like twins. They are not.
In Europe, food agencies treat them as two very different messages. One is about quality. The other is about safety.
So why do food labels have two dates? And where did they come from?
First, the official definitions. Here is how the European Food Safety Authority explains them.
Use by: foods can be eaten until this date but not after, even if they look and smell fine.
Best before, in its words: the food will be safe to eat after this date but may not be at its best.
Spain's food safety agency says it in its own words. Best before is the moment until which a food keeps its expected quality. Use by is the moment until which it can be eaten safely.
This video only repeats what the agencies say, and it is not medical advice. For any real food, read the label and its storage instructions.
Who chooses the label? Food businesses do. The European authority built a decision tool to help food businesses choose between them.
Its questions cover the product itself, how it is handled, and how it is stored.
But where did dates come from? Not, it seems, from a food safety lab.
According to The Spectator, the story starts with the British store Marks and Spencer, in the nineteen fifties.
They began printing dates on food, but only for the stockroom. By nineteen seventy dates were on the shelves, and in nineteen seventy-three the store named them sell-by dates.
Then, in Britain in the nineteen eighties, came the two labels we know today. The Spectator calls best before advisory, and use by a sign of a genuine risk of food poisoning.
That is one account, not a government archive. It suggests dates began as a store tool.
There is also a third date: sell by.
In its published guidance, the United States Department of Agriculture says a sell-by date tells the store how long to display a product. It is not a safety date.
It also says that, except for infant formula, federal rules do not require product dates.
In that guidance, use by means peak quality, not safety, except on infant formula. In Europe, same words, different meaning.
So the sensible habit is to check what the label means in the country where you shop.
Why does it matter? Waste.

In twenty twenty, the European authority wrote that the European Commission estimates up to ten percent of the eighty-eight million metric tons of food waste in the EU each year is linked to date marking.
Linked, not caused. And it is an estimate.

And the story has come full circle. In twenty twenty-two, The Spectator noted that Marks and Spencer said it was dropping sell-by dates on many fruits and vegetables, and going back to stockroom codes.
Now the practical part. This is not medical advice, only how to read a label.
One: find the exact words on the pack. Use by and best before are not the same message.
Two: read the storage instructions on the pack. The European authority's decision tool takes storage conditions into account.
If you are unsure, follow the label and your national food agency, not a guess.
So the two dates are really two questions. Is it safe? And is it at its best?
Labels are not the only small detail nobody explains. Put your hand in your jeans pocket right now.
Feel that tiny pocket inside it? We have already told its story, in another video.
